## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Suññakathā* ("Discussion of Emptiness") is the tenth treatise of the second division (and twentieth treatise overall) of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* [SuttaCentral; Ronkin 2005]. The treatise investigates the qualifier "empty" (*suñña*) and opens by quoting a canonical discourse in which the Venerable Ānanda asks the Buddha why the world is called empty (*suñño loko*), with the Buddha replying that phenomena are empty of a self (*atta*) or anything belonging to a self (*attaniya*) [SuttaCentral; Ronkin 2005]. The text enumerates and defines twenty-five distinct modes of emptiness, including *suñña-suñña* ("empty of emptiness"), which delineates selflessness in connection with the six sense bases [Ñāṇananda 1971]. Across the treatise, the designation of emptiness is systematically applied to 199 individual phenomena [Stanley]. The *Suññakathā* is also philosophically notable for introducing the term *sabhāva* ("individual essence" or "intrinsic nature") into canonical analysis—qualifying born materiality, feeling, and being as "void of individual essence"—which Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli highlighted as an exceptionally rare Piṭaka occurrence of the concept outside the *Buddhavaṁsa* [Ronkin 2005; Stanley].
Curated parallels and intertextual citations link the *Suññakathā* directly to the *Suññatalokasutta* (SN 35.85), the *Attadaṇḍasuttaniddesa* (Mnd 15), the *Mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa* (Cnd 19), the *Puggalakathā* of the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 1.1), and Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* discourse SA 232 [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus corroborates extensive Pali text reuse across 65 texts (1,169 matching passages), sharing large passages particularly with the *Ñāṇakathā* (Ps 1.1), the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35, where §1.4–2.9 aligns with SN 35.85), Cnd 19, Mnd 15, and the *Visuddhimagga* [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus identifies conceptual and textual cross-language alignments with Sanskrit and Tibetan Prajñāpāramitā literature (including the *Daśasāhasrikā* and *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*), Harivarman's *Tattvasiddhiśāstra*, and the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99) [DharmaNexus].
